sections.boxed_warning: WARNING: FETAL TOXICITY. When pregnancy is detected, discontinue Lisinopril as soon as possible. Drugs that act directly on the renin-angiotensin system can cause injury and death to the developing fetus.
sections.indications_and_usage: Lisinopril is an angiotensin converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor indicated for: Treatment of hypertension in adult patients and pediatric patients 6 years of age and older; Adjunctive therapy in heart failure; Treatment of acute myocardial infarction within 24 hours.
sections.dosage_and_administration: Hypertension: Initial adult dose is 10 mg once daily. Titrate up to 40 mg daily based on blood pressure response. Heart Failure: Initial dose is 5 mg once daily with diuretics. Myocardial Infarction: 5 mg within 24 hours, followed by 5 mg after 24 hours, then 10 mg daily for 6 weeks.
sections.contraindications: Lisinopril is contraindicated in patients with a history of angioedema related to previous ACE inhibitor treatment, hereditary or idiopathic angioedema, and co-administration with aliskiren in patients with diabetes.
sections.warnings_and_precautions: Angioedema and Anaphylactoid Reactions: Discontinue Lisinopril immediately. Impaired Renal Function: Monitor serum creatinine periodically. Hyperkalemia: Monitor serum potassium periodically. Hypotension: Risk in volume- or salt-depleted patients.
sections.adverse_reactions: Common adverse reactions (incidence >= 2%) include headache, dizziness, persistent dry cough, fatigue, diarrhea, nausea, and upper respiratory infection.
sections.drug_interactions: Diuretics: Excessive reduction of blood pressure. Potassium-sparing diuretics (spironolactone, triamterene) or potassium supplements: Increased risk of hyperkalemia. NSAIDs: Risk of renal impairment and decreased antihypertensive effect. Lithium: Increased serum lithium levels and toxicity.
sections.use_in_specific_populations: Pregnancy: Discontinue immediately upon pregnancy detection (fetal toxicity). Lactation: Nursing mothers should exercise caution. Pediatric Use: Safety and effectiveness established in patients 6 years and older. Renal Impairment: Reduce initial dose in patients with CrCl < 30 mL/min.
sections.overdosage: Symptoms of overdosage include severe hypotension, electrolyte disturbances, and renal failure. Treatment involves IV infusion of normal saline; lisinopril can be removed by hemodialysis.
sections.clinical_pharmacology: Lisinopril inhibits ACE in human subjects and animals. ACE is a peptidyl dipeptidase that catalyzes the conversion of angiotensin I to the vasoconstrictor substance, angiotensin II. Lisinopril is not bound to other serum proteins and is excreted unchanged entirely in the urine.

sections.boxed_warning: WARNING: FETAL TOXICITY. When pregnancy is detected, discontinue Losartan as soon as possible. Drugs that act directly on the renin-angiotensin system can cause injury and death to the developing fetus.
sections.indications_and_usage: Losartan potassium is an angiotensin II receptor antagonist indicated for: Treatment of hypertension; Reduction of the risk of stroke in patients with hypertension and left ventricular hypertrophy; Treatment of diabetic nephropathy with an elevated serum creatinine and proteinuria in patients with type 2 diabetes and a history of hypertension.
sections.dosage_and_administration: Hypertension: Usual starting dose is 50 mg once daily, with 25 mg used in patients with possible intravascular volume depletion or hepatic impairment. Maximum dose is 100 mg once daily. Diabetic Nephropathy: Starting dose is 50 mg once daily, titrated to 100 mg once daily based on blood pressure response.
sections.contraindications: Hypersensitivity to any component. Do not co-administer aliskiren with Losartan in patients with diabetes.
sections.warnings_and_precautions: Fetal toxicity in pregnancy. Hypotension in volume- or salt-depleted patients. Impaired renal function and hyperkalemia.
sections.adverse_reactions: Most common adverse reactions (incidence >= 1%) include upper respiratory infection, dizziness, nasal congestion, back pain, and fatigue.
sections.drug_interactions: Potassium-sparing diuretics, potassium supplements: May lead to increases in serum potassium. Lithium: Increases in serum lithium concentrations and lithium toxicity reported. NSAIDs: May lead to increased risk of renal impairment and loss of antihypertensive effect.
sections.use_in_specific_populations: Pregnancy: Discontinue immediately upon pregnancy detection. Hepatic Impairment: A 25 mg daily starting dose is recommended for patients with mild-to-moderate hepatic insufficiency.
sections.overdosage: Significant lethality observed in mice/rats. The most likely manifestation of overdosage would be hypotension and tachycardia; bradycardia could occur from parasympathetic stimulation. Treatment is supportive.
sections.clinical_pharmacology: Losartan and its principal active metabolite block the vasoconstrictor and aldosterone-secreting effects of angiotensin II by selectively blocking the binding of angiotensin II to the AT1 receptor found in many tissues.

sections.boxed_warning: WARNING: ISCHEMIC HEART DISEASE. Following abrupt cessation of therapy with certain beta-blocking agents, exacerbations of angina pectoris and, in some cases, myocardial infarction have occurred. When discontinuing chronically administered Lopressor, the dosage should be gradually reduced over a period of 1 - 2 weeks.
sections.indications_and_usage: Metoprolol tartrate is a selective beta-1-adrenoreceptor blocking agent indicated for the treatment of hypertension, angina pectoris, and hemodynamically stable patients with definite or suspected acute myocardial infarction to reduce cardiovascular mortality.
sections.dosage_and_administration: Hypertension: Initial dose is 100 mg daily in single or divided doses, titrated up to 450 mg daily. Angina Pectoris: Initial dose is 100 mg daily given in two divided doses. Myocardial Infarction: In early phase, 3 bolus injections of 5 mg metoprolol IV followed by 50 mg orally every 6 hours for 48 hours.
sections.contraindications: Severe bradycardia, second- or third-degree heart block, cardiogenic shock, decompensated heart failure, sick sinus syndrome, and known hypersensitivity.
sections.warnings_and_precautions: Abrupt cessation may precipitate myocardial infarction. Bradycardia and heart block may worsen. Bronchospastic Disease: In general, patients with bronchospastic disease should not receive beta-blockers. Masking of hypoglycemic symptoms in diabetic patients.
sections.adverse_reactions: Tiredness, dizziness, depression, bradycardia, hypotension, shortness of breath, diarrhea, nausea, and wheezing.
sections.drug_interactions: Catecholamine-depleting drugs (reserpine): Additive hypotension and bradycardia. CYP2D6 Inhibitors (fluoxetine, paroxetine, diphenhydramine): Increase metoprolol plasma concentration. Calcium channel blockers (verapamil, diltiazem): Significant bradycardia and AV conduction depression.
sections.use_in_specific_populations: Pregnancy Category C: Beta-blockers cross placenta and may cause fetal bradycardia. Lactation: Excreted in breast milk in very small quantities. Pediatric Use: Safety and effectiveness not established.
sections.overdosage: Symptoms include severe bradycardia, hypotension, bronchospasm, and acute cardiac failure. Treat with atropine, isoproterenol, glucagon, and cardiac pacing.
sections.clinical_pharmacology: Metoprolol is a beta-1-selective (cardioselective) adrenergic receptor blocking agent. It lacks intrinsic sympathomimetic activity and membrane-stabilizing activity. Extensively metabolized by CYP2D6 in liver.

sections.indications_and_usage: Amlodipine is a dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker indicated for the treatment of hypertension alone or in combination with other antihypertensive agents, and for the management of coronary artery disease (chronic stable angina and vasospastic angina).
sections.dosage_and_administration: Hypertension: Initial adult dose is 5 mg once daily; maximum dose is 10 mg once daily. Small, fragile, or elderly patients or patients with hepatic insufficiency may be started on 2.5 mg once daily. Chronic Stable or Vasospastic Angina: 5-10 mg daily.
sections.contraindications: Known hypersensitivity to amlodipine or any of its components.
sections.warnings_and_precautions: Symptomatic hypotension is possible, particularly in patients with severe aortic stenosis. Worsening angina and acute myocardial infarction can develop after starting or increasing the dose, especially in patients with severe obstructive coronary disease. Peripheral edema may occur.
sections.adverse_reactions: Most common adverse reactions include peripheral edema, dizziness, flushing, palpitations, fatigue, nausea, and somnolence.
sections.drug_interactions: CYP3A4 Inhibitors (ketoconazole, itraconazole, clarithromycin): Increase amlodipine exposure. Simvastatin: Co-administration increases simvastatin exposure (limit simvastatin dose to 20 mg daily with amlodipine). Immunosuppressants (cyclosporine, tacrolimus): Monitor blood levels.
sections.use_in_specific_populations: Pregnancy: Limited human data; use only if potential benefit justifies potential risk. Hepatic Impairment: Dose slowly as amlodipine is extensively metabolized by the liver. Geriatric Use: Start at 2.5 mg daily due to reduced clearance.
sections.overdosage: Overdosage might be expected to cause excessive peripheral vasodilation with marked hypotension and reflex tachycardia. Vasoconstrictors (norepinephrine) and IV calcium gluconate may be beneficial.
sections.clinical_pharmacology: Amlodipine is a peripheral arterial vasodilator that acts directly on vascular smooth muscle to cause reduction in peripheral vascular resistance and reduction in blood pressure. Peak plasma concentrations reached between 6 and 12 hours.

sections.indications_and_usage: Hydrochlorothiazide is a thiazide diuretic indicated as adjunctive therapy in edema associated with congestive heart failure, hepatic cirrhosis, and corticosteroid therapy, and in the management of hypertension as a sole agent or to enhance the effectiveness of other antihypertensives.
sections.dosage_and_administration: Hypertension: Initial dose is 12.5 mg to 25 mg once daily; maximum recommended dose is 50 mg daily. Edema: 25 mg to 100 mg daily in single or divided doses.
sections.contraindications: Anuria. Hypersensitivity to hydrochlorothiazide or other sulfonamide-derived drugs.
sections.warnings_and_precautions: Electrolyte and Metabolic Abnormalities: Hypokalemia, hyponatremia, hypochloremic alkalosis, hypomagnesemia, and hypercalcemia. Hyperuricemia and precipitation of gout. Acute Myopia and Secondary Angle-Closure Glaucoma. Systemic lupus erythematosus exacerbation.
sections.adverse_reactions: Weakness, hypotension including orthostatic hypotension, pancreatitis, jaundice, diarrhea, vomiting, aplastic anemia, leukopenia, purpura, photosensitivity, and muscle spasm.
sections.drug_interactions: Antidiabetic drugs: Dosage adjustment of insulin and oral antidiabetic agents may be required. Lithium: Diuretics reduce the renal clearance of lithium and add a high risk of lithium toxicity. NSAIDs: Can reduce diuretic and antihypertensive effects.
sections.use_in_specific_populations: Pregnancy: Thiazides cross placental barrier; potential risks include fetal jaundice and thrombocytopenia. Renal Impairment: In severe renal disease (CrCl < 30 mL/min), thiazides lose efficacy.
sections.overdosage: Most common signs and symptoms are those caused by electrolyte depletion (hypokalemia, hypochlorema, hyponatremia) and dehydration resulting from excessive diuresis. Treat with fluid and electrolyte replacement.
sections.clinical_pharmacology: Hydrochlorothiazide affects the renal tubular mechanisms of electrolyte reabsorption, directly increasing excretion of sodium and chloride in the distal convoluted tubule. Onset of diuretic action occurs within 2 hours, peaking in 4 hours.

sections.dosage_and_administration: Administer Triamterene/HCTZ orally or as directed. Starting dose is individual based on patient condition, renal and hepatic function, and therapeutic response. Available strengths: 37.5/25 mg, 75/50 mg. Titrate gradually while monitoring clinical efficacy and tolerability.
sections.contraindications: Contraindicated in patients with known hypersensitivity to triamterene and hydrochlorothiazide or any component of the formulation, and in clinical conditions where cardiovascular / potassium-sparing combination diuretic therapy poses severe safety hazards.
sections.warnings_and_precautions: Monitor patients receiving Triamterene/HCTZ for systemic adverse effects, organ toxicity, hypersensitivity reactions, hemodynamic instability, and therapeutic compliance. Perform periodic laboratory monitoring as clinically indicated.
sections.adverse_reactions: The most common adverse reactions reported in clinical trials (>= 2%) include headache, nausea, dizziness, fatigue, gastrointestinal discomfort, somnolence, and formulation-specific reactions.
sections.drug_interactions: Concomitant administration with strong CYP inhibitors, inducers, interacting therapeutic classes, or agents with overlapping toxicities may alter serum concentrations or increase risk of adverse events. Review concurrent medications prior to co-prescribing Triamterene/HCTZ.
sections.use_in_specific_populations: Pregnancy: Assess risk-benefit profile before prescribing. Lactation: Consider benefits of breastfeeding alongside clinical need. Geriatric & Renal/Hepatic Impairment: Dose adjustment and cautious titration recommended.
sections.overdosage: Acute overdosage with Triamterene/HCTZ may result in exaggerated pharmacological effects, hemodynamic compromise, or metabolic derangements. Provide supportive and symptomatic care; monitor vital signs and organ function.
sections.clinical_pharmacology: Triamterene/HCTZ (triamterene and hydrochlorothiazide) exerts its therapeutic effect via targeted action characteristic of Cardiovascular / Potassium-Sparing Combination Diuretic. Pharmacokinetic profile demonstrates predictable absorption, distribution, hepatic/renal metabolism, and clearance.

sections.indications_and_usage: Atorvastatin is an HMG-CoA reductase inhibitor indicated as an adjunct to diet to reduce elevated total cholesterol, LDL-C, apo B, and triglycerides in adults with primary hyperlipidemia, and to reduce the risk of myocardial infarction, stroke, revascularization procedures, and angina in adults with coronary heart disease.
sections.dosage_and_administration: Usual starting dose is 10 mg to 20 mg once daily. For patients who require a large reduction in LDL-C (> 45%), starting dose is 40 mg once daily. Dosage range is 10 mg to 80 mg once daily, taken with or without food at any time of day.
sections.contraindications: Active liver disease, including unexplained persistent elevations in hepatic transaminases. Hypersensitivity to any component of this product. Pregnancy and lactation.
sections.warnings_and_precautions: Myopathy and Rhabdomyolysis: Rare cases of rhabdomyolysis with acute renal failure secondary to myoglobinuria. Discontinue if markedly elevated CPK levels occur or myopathy is diagnosed. Hepatic Dysfunction: Assess liver enzymes before initiating therapy and as clinically indicated.
sections.adverse_reactions: Most common adverse reactions (incidence >= 2%) include nasopharyngitis, arthralgia, diarrhea, pain in extremity, urinary tract infection, and dyspepsia.
sections.drug_interactions: Strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (clarithromycin, itraconazole, protease inhibitors): Greatly increase atorvastatin exposure and rhabdomyolysis risk; adjust or avoid. Gemfibrozil / Fibrates / Niacin: Increased risk of myopathy. Cyclosporine: Avoid concomitant use or limit dose.
sections.use_in_specific_populations: Pregnancy: Contraindicated; statins decrease cholesterol synthesis essential for fetal development. Lactation: Contraindicated. Females of Reproductive Potential: Use effective contraception.
sections.overdosage: There is no specific treatment for atorvastatin overdosage. If an overdose occurs, treat symptomatically and institute supportive measures. Hemodialysis is not expected to significantly enhance clearance.
sections.clinical_pharmacology: Atorvastatin is a selective, competitive inhibitor of HMG-CoA reductase, the rate-limiting enzyme that converts 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-coenzyme A to mevalonate, a precursor of sterols including cholesterol. Extensively metabolized by CYP3A4.

sections.boxed_warning: WARNING: LACTIC ACIDOSIS. Post-marketing cases of metformin-associated lactic acidosis have resulted in death, hypothermia, hypotension, and resistant bradyarrhythmias. Risk factors include renal impairment, concomitant use of certain drugs (e.g., carbonic anhydrase inhibitors), age 65 or greater, radiological studies with iodinated contrast, surgery, hypoxic states, and excessive alcohol intake. If lactic acidosis is suspected, immediately discontinue Metformin and institute prompt hemodialysis.
sections.indications_and_usage: Metformin hydrochloride is a biguanide indicated as an adjunct to diet and exercise to improve glycemic control in adults and pediatric patients 10 years of age and older with type 2 diabetes mellitus.
sections.dosage_and_administration: Adult Starting Dose: 500 mg orally twice a day with meals or 850 mg once a day. Titrate by 500 mg weekly or 850 mg every 2 weeks up to a maximum daily dose of 2000 mg to 2550 mg in divided doses. Pediatric (10-16 yrs): 500 mg twice daily up to 2000 mg daily.
sections.contraindications: Severe renal impairment (eGFR below 30 mL/min/1.73 m²). Known hypersensitivity to metformin. Acute or chronic metabolic acidosis, including diabetic ketoacidosis.
sections.warnings_and_precautions: Lactic Acidosis risk. Renal Impairment: Assess renal function prior to initiation and periodically thereafter. Iodinated Contrast: Discontinue metformin at the time of or prior to iodinated contrast imaging in patients with eGFR between 30 and 60 mL/min. Vitamin B12 Deficiency: Metformin may lower vitamin B12 levels; monitor hematologic parameters annually.
sections.adverse_reactions: Most common adverse reactions (incidence > 5%) are diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, flatulence, abdominal discomfort, indigestion, asthenia, and headache.
sections.drug_interactions: Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (topiramate, zonisamide): Increase risk of lactic acidosis. Cationic drugs eliminated by renal tubular secretion (cimetidine, ranolazine, dolutegravir): May increase metformin plasma concentrations. Alcohol: Potentiates metformin effect on lactate metabolism.
sections.use_in_specific_populations: Pregnancy: Limited available data; poorly controlled diabetes in pregnancy increases risks for mother and fetus. Renal Impairment: Contraindicated in eGFR < 30 mL/min; not recommended to initiate if eGFR between 30-45 mL/min. Geriatric Use: Assess renal function frequently.
sections.overdosage: Overdose of metformin has occurred, leading to lactic acidosis in approximately 10% of cases. Hemodialysis is the most effective method for removal of metformin and correction of acidosis.
sections.clinical_pharmacology: Metformin decreases hepatic glucose production, decreases intestinal absorption of glucose, and improves insulin sensitivity by increasing peripheral glucose uptake and utilization. Metformin is not metabolized by the liver and is cleared by renal excretion.

sections.indications_and_usage: Empagliflozin is an SGLT2 inhibitor indicated: As an adjunct to diet and exercise to improve glycemic control in adults and pediatric patients aged 10 years and older with type 2 diabetes; To reduce the risk of cardiovascular death in adults with type 2 diabetes and established cardiovascular disease; To reduce the risk of cardiovascular death and hospitalization for heart failure in adults with heart failure; To reduce the risk of sustained eGFR decline in adults with chronic kidney disease.
sections.dosage_and_administration: The recommended dose of empagliflozin is 10 mg once daily in the morning, taken with or without food. In patients tolerating 10 mg daily who require additional glycemic control, the dose may be increased to 25 mg once daily. Assess renal function before initiation.
sections.contraindications: Severe hypersensitivity reaction to empagliflozin or any excipients. Patients on dialysis.
sections.warnings_and_precautions: Ketoacidosis: Serious, life-threatening cases of ketoacidosis in type 1 and type 2 diabetes regardless of blood glucose levels (euglycemic ketoacidosis). Volume Depletion: Symptomatic hypotension can occur, particularly in patients with renal impairment, elderly patients, or patients on loop diuretics. Urosepsis and Pyelonephritis: Serious urinary tract infections. Necrotizing Fasciitis of the Perineum (Fournier's Gangrene): Rare life-threatening bacterial infection. Lower Limb Amputation risk.
sections.adverse_reactions: Urinary tract infections, female genital mycotic infections, upper respiratory tract infections, increased urination, dyslipidemia, arthralgia, and thirst.
sections.drug_interactions: Co-administration with insulin or insulin secretagogues increases the risk of hypoglycemia; a lower dose of insulin or secretagogue may be required. Co-administration with diuretics causes additive volume depletion and hypotension.
sections.use_in_specific_populations: Pregnancy: Not recommended during the second and third trimesters of pregnancy due to potential risk to fetal renal development. Lactation: Not recommended. Renal Impairment: Initiation not recommended if eGFR < 20 mL/min/1.73 m².
sections.overdosage: In the event of an overdose, employ the usual supportive measures as dictated by the patient's clinical status. Removal of empagliflozin by hemodialysis has not been studied.
sections.clinical_pharmacology: Sodium-glucose co-transporter 2 (SGLT2) is the predominant transporter responsible for reabsorption of glucose from the glomerular filtrate back into the circulation. Empagliflozin reduces renal reabsorption of filtered glucose and lowers the renal threshold for glucose, increasing urinary glucose excretion.

sections.indications_and_usage: Glipizide is a second-generation sulfonylurea indicated as an adjunct to diet and exercise to improve glycemic control in adults with type 2 diabetes mellitus.
sections.dosage_and_administration: Immediate-Release: Starting dose is 5 mg daily given before breakfast. Titrate in increments of 2.5 to 5 mg up to a maximum recommended single dose of 15 mg or total daily dose of 40 mg. Extended-Release (XL): Starting dose is 5 mg once daily with breakfast, maximum 20 mg daily.
sections.contraindications: Known hypersensitivity to glipizide or sulfonamides. Type 1 diabetes mellitus and diabetic ketoacidosis.
sections.warnings_and_precautions: Hypoglycemia: All sulfonylurea drugs are capable of producing severe hypoglycemia; elderly, debilitated, or malnourished patients and those with adrenal or renal insufficiency are particularly susceptible. Hemolytic Anemia: In patients with G6PD deficiency, sulfonylureas can cause hemolytic anemia. Increased risk of cardiovascular mortality based on UGDP study.
sections.adverse_reactions: Hypoglycemia, dizziness, diarrhea, nervousness, flatulence, tremor, skin rash, pruritus, and urticaria.
sections.drug_interactions: Certain drugs tend to produce hypoglycemia and potentiate glipizide action: NSAIDs, salicylates, sulfonamides, chloramphenicol, probenecid, coumarins, MAOIs, and beta-blockers. Drugs that produce hyperglycemia and decrease control: Thiazide diuretics, corticosteroids, phenothiazines, thyroid hormones, estrogens, and oral contraceptives.
sections.use_in_specific_populations: Pregnancy: Prolonged severe hypoglycemia has been reported in neonates born to mothers receiving sulfonylurea at delivery; discontinue at least 2 weeks before expected delivery. Renal/Hepatic Impairment: Initial dose should be 2.5 mg daily.
sections.overdosage: Mild hypoglycemia without loss of consciousness is treated with oral glucose. Severe hypoglycemic reactions with coma or neurological impairment require immediate hospitalization and IV 50% glucose followed by continuous 10% glucose infusion.
sections.clinical_pharmacology: The primary mechanism of action of glipizide appears to be the stimulation of insulin secretion from the beta cells of pancreatic islet tissue, dependent on functioning beta cells. Extensively metabolized by the liver, primarily via CYP2C9.

sections.boxed_warning: WARNING: NOT FOR TREATMENT OF OBESITY OR FOR WEIGHT LOSS. Thyroid hormones, including Synthroid, either alone or with other therapeutic agents, should not be used for the treatment of obesity or for weight loss. In euthyroid patients, doses within the range of daily hormonal requirements are ineffective for weight reduction. Larger doses may produce serious or even life-threatening manifestations of toxicity, particularly when given in association with sympathomimetic amines such as those used for their anorectic effects.
sections.indications_and_usage: Synthroid (levothyroxine sodium) is indicated for: Replacement therapy in primary (thyroidal), secondary (pituitary), and tertiary (hypothalamic) congenital or acquired hypothyroidism; Pituitary Thyrotropin (TSH) Suppression as an adjunct to surgery and radioiodine therapy in the management of thyrotropin-dependent well-differentiated thyroid cancer.
sections.dosage_and_administration: Administer once daily as a single dose, on an empty stomach, one-half to one hour before breakfast with a full glass of water. Full replacement dose in adult patients with primary hypothyroidism without cardiac disease is approximately 1.6 mcg/kg/day. In elderly patients or patients with underlying cardiovascular disease, start at 12.5 to 25 mcg/day and titrate every 6-8 weeks based on serum TSH.
sections.contraindications: Uncorrected adrenal insufficiency (thyroid hormone increases metabolic clearance of glucocorticoids and may precipitate an acute adrenal crisis). Hypersensitivity to synthetic levothyroxine.
sections.warnings_and_precautions: Cardiac Adverse Reactions in the Elderly and in Patients with Underlying Cardiovascular Disease (angina, arrhythmias, myocardial infarction). Myxedema Coma requires IV levothyroxine, not oral. Acute Adrenal Crisis in patients with concomitant adrenal insufficiency. Worsening Diabetic Control: May increase insulin or antidiabetic agent requirements. Decreased bone mineral density with overtreatment.
sections.adverse_reactions: Adverse reactions of Synthroid are primarily those of hyperthyroidism due to therapeutic overdosage: arrhythmias, tachycardia, palpitation, myocardial infarction, dyspnea, muscle spasms, headache, nervousness, irritability, insomnia, tremors, muscle weakness, increased appetite, weight loss, diarrhea, heat intolerance, and menstrual irregularities.
sections.drug_interactions: Calcium carbonate, ferrous sulfate, bile acid sequestrants (cholestyramine, colestipol), sucralfate, aluminum antacids, and proton pump inhibitors: Bind levothyroxine and markedly reduce absorption; separate administration by at least 4 hours. Warfarin: Levothyroxine increases catabolism of vitamin K-dependent clotting factors, potentiating anticoagulant effect. Digoxin: Thyroid hormone increases renal clearance of digoxin.
sections.use_in_specific_populations: Pregnancy: Thyroid requirements frequently increase during pregnancy; monitor TSH every trimester and adjust dose promptly. Hypothyroidism during pregnancy increases risk of spontaneous abortion, preeclampsia, and impaired fetal neurological development. Lactation: Minimal excretion into breast milk. Pediatric: Dosing is higher per kg (e.g., 10-15 mcg/kg/day in neonates).
sections.overdosage: Signs and symptoms of overdose are those of hyperthyroidism and thyroid storm (agitation, confusion, tachycardia, hyperthermia, arrhythmias). Treat with beta-blockers (propranolol) to counteract increased sympathetic tone, oxygen, and supportive care.
sections.clinical_pharmacology: Levothyroxine (T4) is a synthetic form of thyroxine that undergoes peripheral deiodination to triiodothyronine (T3), which enters the cell nucleus and binds to thyroid hormone receptors to initiate transcription of metabolic proteins. Circulating T4 is > 99% protein-bound to thyroxine-binding globulin (TBG).

sections.indications_and_usage: Prednisone is a synthetic glucocorticoid indicated for: Endocrine disorders (adrenal insufficiency); Rheumatic disorders (rheumatoid arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis); Collagen diseases (systemic lupus erythematosus, acute rheumatic carditis); Dermatologic diseases (pemphigus, severe erythema multiforme); Allergic states (severe asthma, contact dermatitis); Ophthalmic diseases; Respiratory diseases; Hematologic disorders (autoimmune hemolytic anemia); Neoplastic diseases (leukemias and lymphomas); Edematous states (nephrotic syndrome); Acute exacerbations of multiple sclerosis.
sections.dosage_and_administration: Initial dosage may vary from 5 mg to 60 mg per day depending on the specific disease entity being treated. In situations of less severity, lower doses will generally suffice, while in selected patients higher initial doses may be required. When discontinuing prolonged therapy, the dosage must be tapered gradually rather than stopped abruptly to prevent secondary adrenocortical insufficiency.
sections.contraindications: Systemic fungal infections. Known hypersensitivity to prednisone or its components.
sections.warnings_and_precautions: Hypothalamic-Pituitary-Adrenal (HPA) Axis Suppression and Acute Adrenal Crisis upon abrupt withdrawal. Immunosuppression and Increased Risk of Infections: Glucocorticoids mask signs of infection and new infections may appear during use; chickenpox and measles can have serious/fatal course in non-immune patients. Peptic Ulceration and Gastrointestinal Perforation. Ophthalmic Effects: Cataracts, glaucoma, and ocular infections. Osteoporosis and Aseptic Necrosis of bone. Psychiatric Disturbances (euphoria, insomnia, mood swings, psychosis). Hyperglycemia and worsening diabetes. Fluid retention and hypertension.
sections.adverse_reactions: Fluid retention, sodium retention, potassium loss, hypokalemic alkalosis, muscle weakness, osteoporosis, peptic ulcer, pancreatitis, cushingoid state, growth suppression in children, impaired wound healing, thin fragile skin, petechiae, facial erythema, convulsions, vertigo, headache, and menstrual irregularities.
sections.drug_interactions: NSAIDs (aspirin, ibuprofen): Concomitant use increases risk of gastrointestinal ulceration and bleeding. Antidiabetic agents: Glucocorticoids raise blood glucose; antidiabetic dose increase required. Phenytoin, Phenobarbital, Rifampin: CYP3A4 inducers increase hepatic metabolism of prednisone and decrease efficacy. Live Vaccines: Live virus vaccines are contraindicated in patients receiving immunosuppressive doses of corticosteroids.
sections.use_in_specific_populations: Pregnancy Category C: Hypoadrenalism may occur in infants born of mothers who have received substantial doses of corticosteroids during pregnancy. Nursing Mothers: Excreted in breast milk and could suppress growth or interfere with endogenous corticosteroid production. Pediatric Use: Growth and development should be carefully monitored.
sections.overdosage: Acute overdosage is unlikely to produce life-threatening symptoms. Chronic overdose leads to typical signs of Cushing's syndrome (moon face, buffalo hump, central obesity, striae, osteoporosis, hypertension, hyperglycemia). Treat by gradual reduction of dosage.
sections.clinical_pharmacology: Prednisone is a synthetic adrenocortical steroid with potent glucocorticoid properties. It is converted in the liver to its active metabolite, prednisolone. It decreases inflammation by suppressing migration of polymorphonuclear leukocytes and reversing increased capillary permeability.

sections.indications_and_usage: Amoxicillin is a penicillin-class antibacterial indicated for the treatment of infections due to susceptible isolates of designated microorganisms in: Infections of the ear, nose, and throat (Streptococcus spp., S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae); Infections of the genitourinary tract (E. coli, P. mirabilis, E. faecalis); Infections of the skin and skin structure; Lower respiratory tract infections; Triple therapy for Helicobacter pylori eradication.
sections.dosage_and_administration: Adults: 500 mg every 12 hours or 250 mg every 8 hours for mild-to-moderate infections. For severe infections, 875 mg every 12 hours or 500 mg every 8 hours. Pediatric Patients (> 3 months): 20 to 45 mg/kg/day in divided doses every 8 or 12 hours.
sections.contraindications: Known serious hypersensitivity reaction (e.g., anaphylaxis or Stevens-Johnson syndrome) to amoxicillin or other beta-lactam antibacterial drugs (e.g., penicillins and cephalosporins).
sections.warnings_and_precautions: Serious and occasionally fatal hypersensitivity (anaphylactic) reactions have been reported in patients on penicillin therapy. Clostridioides difficile-associated diarrhea (CDAD) ranging from mild diarrhea to fatal colitis. Development of drug-resistant bacteria if prescribed without proven bacterial infection. Rash in patients with mononucleosis.
sections.adverse_reactions: Most common adverse reactions (> 1%) are diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, skin rashes, urticaria, and vaginitis.
sections.drug_interactions: Probenecid: Decreases renal tubular secretion of amoxicillin, producing higher and prolonged blood levels. Oral Anticoagulants (warfarin): May prolong prothrombin time; monitor INR closely. Allopurinol: Concomitant administration substantially increases the incidence of skin rashes. Oral Contraceptives: May decrease contraceptive efficacy.
sections.use_in_specific_populations: Pregnancy Category B: Penicillins generally considered safe in pregnancy; use only if clearly needed. Nursing Mothers: Amoxicillin is excreted in human milk; may cause diarrhea or sensitization in infants. Renal Impairment: In patients with GFR 10 to 30 mL/min, dose is 250-500 mg every 12 hours; if GFR < 10 mL/min, 250-500 mg every 24 hours.
sections.overdosage: In case of overdose, discontinue medication, treat symptomatically, and institute supportive measures. Interstitial nephritis and oliguric renal failure have been reported. Amoxicillin can be removed by hemodialysis.
sections.clinical_pharmacology: Amoxicillin is a bactericidal antibiotic that acts by inhibiting the synthesis of bacterial cell-wall mucopeptides during active multiplication. It is stable in the presence of gastric acid and is rapidly absorbed after oral administration.

sections.boxed_warning: WARNING: SERIOUS ADVERSE REACTIONS INCLUDING TENDINITIS, TENDON RUPTURE, PERIPHERAL NEUROPATHY, CENTRAL NERVOUS SYSTEM EFFECTS AND EXACERBATION OF MYASTHENIA GRAVIS. Fluoroquinolones, including Ciprofloxacin, have been associated with disabling and potentially irreversible serious adverse reactions that have occurred together including tendinitis and tendon rupture, peripheral neuropathy, and CNS effects. Discontinue Ciprofloxacin immediately if a patient experiences any of these serious adverse reactions. In patients with myasthenia gravis, fluoroquinolones may exacerbate muscle weakness. Avoid ciprofloxacin in patients with known history of myasthenia gravis.
sections.indications_and_usage: Ciprofloxacin is a fluoroquinolone antibacterial indicated in adults for the treatment of urinary tract infections, chronic bacterial prostatitis, lower respiratory tract infections, acute sinusitis, skin and skin structure infections, bone and joint infections, complicated intra-abdominal infections, infectious diarrhea, and post-exposure inhalational anthrax.
sections.dosage_and_administration: Urinary Tract Infections: 250 mg to 500 mg orally every 12 hours for 7 to 14 days. Lower Respiratory / Skin / Bone: 500 mg to 750 mg orally every 12 hours for 7 to 14 days (up to 4-6 weeks for bone infections). Post-exposure Anthrax: 500 mg orally every 12 hours for 60 days.
sections.contraindications: Known hypersensitivity to ciprofloxacin or any other quinolones. Concomitant administration with tizanidine (causes severe hypotension and sedation due to CYP1A2 inhibition).
sections.warnings_and_precautions: Disabling and potentially irreversible serious adverse reactions (tendon rupture, neuropathy, CNS toxicities including seizures, psychosis, and toxic psychosis). Aortic aneurysm and dissection: Increased risk within 2 months of use. Blood glucose disturbances: Hypoglycemia coma reported in elderly diabetics. QT prolongation.
sections.adverse_reactions: Nausea, diarrhea, liver function test abnormalities, vomiting, rash, headache, restlessness, insomnia, and abdominal pain.
sections.drug_interactions: Tizanidine: Contraindicated (CYP1A2 inhibition). Theophylline: Significant increase in theophylline toxicity; monitor blood levels. Multivalent Cation-Containing Products (antacids with magnesium/aluminum, iron supplements, calcium, dairy): Markedly reduce ciprofloxacin absorption; administer ciprofloxacin at least 2 hours before or 6 hours after.
sections.use_in_specific_populations: Pregnancy: Quinolones cause arthropathy in juvenile animals; use only if potential benefit justifies potential risk. Pediatric Use: Not drug of first choice due to increased incidence of adverse musculoskeletal events (arthralgia, tendonitis). Renal Impairment: Dose reduction required if CrCl < 50 mL/min.
sections.overdosage: In the event of acute overdosage, reversible renal toxicity has been reported. Empty the stomach by inducing vomiting or gastric lavage; maintain hydration. Only a small amount (< 10%) is removed by hemodialysis.
sections.clinical_pharmacology: Bactericidal action of ciprofloxacin results from inhibition of topoisomerase II (DNA gyrase) and topoisomerase IV, which are required for bacterial DNA replication, transcription, repair, and recombination.

sections.indications_and_usage: Azithromycin is a macrolide antibacterial indicated for mild to moderate infections caused by designated susceptible bacteria in: Acute bacterial exacerbations of chronic bronchitis; Acute bacterial sinusitis; Community-acquired pneumonia; Pharyngitis/tonsillitis; Uncomplicated skin and skin structure infections; Urethritis and cervicitis due to Chlamydia trachomatis; Genital ulcer disease in men due to Haemophilus ducreyi.
sections.dosage_and_administration: Community-Acquired Pneumonia / Skin Infections: 500 mg as a single dose on Day 1, followed by 250 mg once daily on Days 2 through 5 (Z-Pak regimen). Acute Sinusitis: 500 mg once daily for 3 days. Genital Chlamydial Infection: Single 1 gram (1000 mg) dose.
sections.contraindications: Hypersensitivity to azithromycin, erythromycin, or any macrolide or ketolide. History of cholestatic jaundice or hepatic dysfunction associated with prior use of azithromycin.
sections.warnings_and_precautions: QT Interval Prolongation: Can cause prolonged cardiac repolarization and QT interval, imparting risk of cardiac arrhythmia and torsades de pointes. Fatalities reported in elderly patients and those with preexisting cardiac risk factors. Hepatotoxicity: Abnormal liver function, hepatitis, cholestatic jaundice, hepatic necrosis, and hepatic failure reported. Infantile Hypertrophic Pyloric Stenosis (IHPS). Clostridioides difficile-associated diarrhea (CDAD).
sections.adverse_reactions: Diarrhea/loose stools, nausea, abdominal pain, vomiting, headache, dizziness, and vaginitis.
sections.drug_interactions: Nelfinavir: Increases azithromycin serum concentrations. Warfarin: Monitor prothrombin time/INR. Digoxin, Colchicine: Concomitant administration with macrolides can elevate serum levels of P-gp substrates. Drugs prolonging QT interval (amiodarone, quinidine, sotalol): Increased risk of fatal arrhythmias.
sections.use_in_specific_populations: Pregnancy Category B: Studies in animals show no evidence of harm to fetus. Nursing: Azithromycin is excreted in human breast milk. Geriatric Use: Elderly patients may be more susceptible to drug-associated effects on the QT interval.
sections.overdosage: Adverse reactions experienced in higher than recommended doses were similar to those seen at normal doses. In the event of overdose, general symptomatic and supportive measures are indicated.
sections.clinical_pharmacology: Azithromycin binds to the 23S rRNA of the 50S ribosomal subunit of susceptible microorganisms, inhibiting protein synthesis by interfering with the transpeptidation/translocation step. Characterized by rapid tissue penetration and high intracellular concentrations.

sections.indications_and_usage: Albuterol sulfate inhalation aerosol is a beta-2-adrenergic agonist indicated for: Treatment or prevention of bronchospasm in adult and pediatric patients aged 4 years and older with reversible obstructive airway disease (asthma, COPD); Prevention of exercise-induced bronchospasm (EIB) in patients aged 4 years and older.
sections.dosage_and_administration: Acute Bronchospasm: 2 inhalations (180 mcg) every 4 to 6 hours as needed. Prevention of Exercise-Induced Bronchospasm: 2 inhalations 15 to 30 minutes before exercise. Prime the inhaler before first use and when inhaler has not been used for > 2 weeks.
sections.contraindications: Hypersensitivity to albuterol or any of the ingredients.
sections.warnings_and_precautions: Paradoxical Bronchospasm: Life-threatening paradoxical bronchospasm may occur with acute wheezing; discontinue immediately and treat with alternative therapy. Cardiovascular Effects: Produces clinically significant cardiovascular effects in some patients as measured by pulse rate, blood pressure, and ECG changes (tachycardia, palpitations, arrhythmias). Immediate Hypersensitivity Reactions. Hypokalemia and Hyperglycemia. Excessive use can be fatal.
sections.adverse_reactions: Tremor, nervousness, headache, dizziness, insomnia, tachycardia, palpitations, nausea, vomiting, throat irritation, upper respiratory tract infection, and cough.
sections.drug_interactions: Beta-Blockers (propranolol): Inhibit the bronchodilator effect of albuterol and may produce severe bronchospasm in patients with asthma. Diuretics: Non-potassium-sparing diuretics (loop or thiazides) can worsen ECG changes and hypokalemia. Digoxin: May decrease serum digoxin levels. Monoamine Oxidase Inhibitors (MAOIs) and Tricyclic Antidepressants (TCAs): Potentiate action of albuterol on cardiovascular system.
sections.use_in_specific_populations: Pregnancy Category C: Animal reproduction studies have shown teratogenic effects in mice; use during pregnancy only if potential benefit justifies potential risk. Labor and Delivery: Oral albuterol inhibits uterine contractions. Nursing Mothers: Not known whether albuterol is excreted in human milk.
sections.overdosage: The expected signs of overdosage are those of excessive beta-adrenergic stimulation (seizures, angina, hypertension or hypotension, tachycardia with rates up to 200 beats per minute, arrhythmias, nervousness, headache, tremor, dry mouth, nausea, dizziness, fatigue, and hypokalemia). Cardiac arrest and death may occur. Treat with judicious use of cardioselective beta-blocker.
sections.clinical_pharmacology: Albuterol is a sympathomimetic amine that acts selectively on beta-2-adrenergic receptors of bronchial smooth muscle to increase cyclic AMP, activating protein kinase A and inhibiting phosphorylation of myosin, resulting in smooth muscle relaxation and bronchodilation.

sections.indications_and_usage: Gabapentin is indicated for: Management of postherpetic neuralgia in adults; Adjunctive therapy in the treatment of partial onset seizures, with and without secondary generalization, in adults and pediatric patients 3 years of age and older with epilepsy.
sections.dosage_and_administration: Postherpetic Neuralgia: Day 1: 300 mg once daily; Day 2: 300 mg twice daily; Day 3: 300 mg three times daily. Titrate up to 1800 mg/day (600 mg three times daily). Epilepsy (Adults): Starting dose is 300 mg three times daily. Maintenance dose is 900 to 1800 mg/day in three divided doses; maximum dose is 2400 to 3600 mg/day. Dose must be adjusted in patients with reduced renal function (CrCl < 60 mL/min).
sections.contraindications: Known hypersensitivity to gabapentin or its ingredients.
sections.warnings_and_precautions: Antiepileptic Drugs (AEDs) and Suicidal Behavior: Increases the risk of suicidal thoughts or behavior. Monitor for depression or unusual mood changes. Respiratory Depression: Serious, life-threatening hypoventilation when co-administered with central nervous system (CNS) depressants (opioids) or in patients with underlying respiratory impairment. Somnolence and Dizziness: Impairs ability to drive or operate machinery. Drug Reaction with Eosinophilia and Systemic Symptoms (DRESS / Multiorgan Hypersensitivity). Abrupt discontinuation may increase seizure frequency.
sections.adverse_reactions: Most common adverse reactions in postherpetic neuralgia: dizziness, somnolence, peripheral edema, infection, ataxia, and blurred vision. In epilepsy: somnolence, dizziness, ataxia, fatigue, and nystagmus.
sections.drug_interactions: Opioids (morphine, oxycodone): Co-administration increases gabapentin concentrations and markedly increases risk of CNS depression and fatal respiratory depression. Antacids (Maalox): Reduce gabapentin bioavailability by about 20%; take gabapentin at least 2 hours after antacid.
sections.use_in_specific_populations: Pregnancy Category C: Use during pregnancy only if the potential benefit justifies the potential risk to the fetus. Nursing Mothers: Gabapentin is secreted into human milk. Renal Impairment: Dosage adjustment required based on creatinine clearance.
sections.overdosage: Acute toxicity with doses up to 49 grams has been observed. Symptoms include double vision, slurred speech, drowsiness, lethargy, diarrhea, and marked sedation. Hemodialysis can remove gabapentin and may be indicated in patients with renal impairment.
sections.clinical_pharmacology: Gabapentin is structurally related to the neurotransmitter gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) but does not bind to GABA receptors or influence GABA uptake/metabolism. Gabapentin binds with high affinity to the alpha-2-delta subunit of voltage-gated calcium channels in the CNS, reducing the release of excitatory neurotransmitters. Eliminated solely by renal excretion.

sections.indications_and_usage: Levetiracetam is an antiepileptic drug indicated for: Adjunctive therapy in the treatment of partial-onset seizures in patients 1 month of age and older; Adjunctive therapy in the treatment of myoclonic seizures in patients 12 years of age and older with juvenile myoclonic epilepsy; Adjunctive therapy in the treatment of primary generalized tonic-clonic seizures in patients 6 years of age and older with idiopathic generalized epilepsy.
sections.dosage_and_administration: Adults (16 years and older): Initiate treatment with a daily dose of 1000 mg/day, given as 500 mg twice daily. Increase dose by 1000 mg/day every 2 weeks up to a maximum recommended daily dose of 3000 mg/day (1500 mg twice daily). Renal impairment: Adjust dose based on creatinine clearance (e.g., CrCl 50-80 mL/min: 500-1000 mg q12h; CrCl < 30 mL/min: 250-500 mg q12h).
sections.contraindications: Known hypersensitivity to levetiracetam; angioedema and anaphylaxis have occurred.
sections.warnings_and_precautions: Behavioral Abnormalities and Psychotic Symptoms: May cause somnolence, fatigue, irritability, aggression, agitation, anger, depression, and psychosis. Suicidal Behavior and Ideation: Monitor for emergence of suicidal thoughts. Serious Dermatologic Reactions: Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS) and toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN). Anaphylaxis and Angioedema. Withdrawal Seizures: As with all AEDs, withdraw gradually.
sections.adverse_reactions: Somnolence, asthenia, infection, dizziness, nasopharyngitis, fatigue, decreased appetite, irritability, and headache.
sections.drug_interactions: Levetiracetam does not inhibit or induce hepatic cytochrome P450 enzymes. No significant pharmacokinetic interactions observed with other antiepileptic drugs (phenytoin, carbamazepine, valproate, lamotrigine, gabapentin, phenobarbital). Probenecid: Inhibits renal tubular clearance of levetiracetam metabolite.
sections.use_in_specific_populations: Pregnancy Category C: North American Antiepileptic Drug (NAAED) Pregnancy Registry data indicates no major increase in congenital malformations compared to baseline. Nursing Mothers: Levetiracetam is excreted in human breast milk. Renal Impairment: Renal clearance is decreased in patients with renal disease; dosage adjustment is required.
sections.overdosage: Highest known dose was 60 g. Symptoms include somnolence, agitation, aggression, depressed level of consciousness, respiratory depression, and coma. Emesis or gastric lavage; hemodialysis removes approximately 50% of body levetiracetam in 4 hours.
sections.clinical_pharmacology: The precise mechanism by which levetiracetam exerts its antiepileptic action is unknown. Levetiracetam binds selectively to the synaptic vesicle protein 2A (SV2A) in the brain, which is believed to be involved in vesicle exocytosis and modulation of neurotransmitter release. Rapidly absorbed with minimal protein binding (< 10%).

sections.boxed_warning: WARNING: SUICIDAL THOUGHTS AND BEHAVIORS. Antidepressants increased the risk of suicidal thoughts and behaviors in pediatric and young adult patients in short-term studies. Closely monitor all antidepressant-treated patients for clinical worsening, and for emergence of suicidal thoughts and behaviors. Sertraline is not approved for use in pediatric patients except for patients with obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD).
sections.indications_and_usage: Sertraline hydrochloride is a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI) indicated for the treatment of: Major depressive disorder (MDD); Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) in adults and pediatric patients aged 6 years and older; Panic disorder; Post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD); Social anxiety disorder (SAD); Premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD).
sections.dosage_and_administration: Administer once daily, morning or evening. MDD and OCD: Starting dose is 50 mg once daily. Panic Disorder, PTSD, and SAD: Starting dose is 25 mg once daily, increased to 50 mg once daily after one week. Maximum dose is 200 mg once daily. PMDD: 50 mg/day either continuously or during luteal phase.
sections.contraindications: Concomitant use of monoamine oxidase inhibitors (MAOIs) or within 14 days of discontinuing an MAOI (causes fatal serotonin syndrome). Concomitant use of pimozide (increases pimozide levels and QT prolongation). Known hypersensitivity to sertraline.
sections.warnings_and_precautions: Suicidal thoughts and behaviors. Serotonin Syndrome: Potentially life-threatening when used with other serotonergic agents (triptans, tricyclic antidepressants, fentanyl, lithium, tramadol, buspirone, amphetamines, St. John's Wort). Increased Risk of Bleeding: Inhibit platelet serotonin reuptake; additive risk with NSAIDs, aspirin, or warfarin. Activation of Mania/Hypomania in bipolar disorder. Seizures. Angle-Closure Glaucoma. Hyponatremia / SIADH. Sexual Dysfunction. Discontinuation Syndrome upon abrupt cessation.
sections.adverse_reactions: Most common adverse reactions (incidence >= 5% and twice placebo): nausea, diarrhea/loose stools, tremor, dyspepsia, decreased appetite, hyperhidrosis, ejaculation failure, and insomnia.
sections.drug_interactions: MAOIs: Contraindicated (serotonin syndrome). Pimozide: Contraindicated. Drugs affecting hemostasis (NSAIDs, aspirin, warfarin): Increase risk of bleeding. Serotonergic Drugs: Increase serotonin syndrome risk. CYP2D6 Substrates (propafenone, flecainide, TCAs): Sertraline can increase plasma levels.
sections.use_in_specific_populations: Pregnancy: Third trimester exposure increases risk of persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn (PPHN) and neonatal adaptation syndrome. Nursing Mothers: Sertraline is excreted into human breast milk. Pediatric Use: Safety and effectiveness established only in OCD patients aged 6 to 17 years. Hepatic Impairment: Use lower or less frequent dosage.
sections.overdosage: Overdoses of up to 13.5 grams have been reported. Symptoms include somnolence, gastrointestinal disturbances (nausea, vomiting), tachycardia, tremor, agitation, dizziness, and serotonin syndrome. Treat with airway management, oxygenation, cardiac monitoring, and supportive care; no specific antidote.
sections.clinical_pharmacology: The mechanism of action of sertraline is presumed to be linked to its potent and selective inhibition of CNS neuronal uptake of serotonin (5-HT). It has only very weak effects on norepinephrine and dopamine neuronal reuptake. Extensively metabolized by the liver, primarily by CYP2B6, CYP2C19, CYP2C9, CYP3A4, and CYP2D6.

sections.indications_and_usage: Cymbalta is a serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor (SNRI) indicated for: Major Depressive Disorder (MDD); Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD) in adults and pediatric patients aged 7 years and older; Diabetic Peripheral Neuropathic Pain (DPNP); Fibromyalgia; Chronic Musculoskeletal Pain (chronic lower back pain and chronic osteoarthritis pain).
sections.dosage_and_administration: Administer orally with or without food. Swallow capsules whole; do not chew, crush, or open. MDD: 40 mg/day (20 mg twice daily) to 60 mg/day (once daily or 30 mg twice daily); maximum dose 120 mg/day. GAD: 60 mg once daily. DPNP: 60 mg once daily. Fibromyalgia: 60 mg once daily. Chronic Musculoskeletal Pain: 60 mg once daily. Discontinue gradually.
sections.contraindications: Concomitant use of monoamine oxidase inhibitors (MAOIs) or within 14 days of stopping an MAOI (serotonin syndrome). Concomitant use with linezolid or methylene blue. Known hypersensitivity to duloxetine.
sections.warnings_and_precautions: Hepatotoxicity: Hepatic failure, sometimes fatal, reported; avoid in patients with substantial alcohol use or chronic liver disease. Orthostatic Hypotension, Falls, and Syncope: Blood pressure and heart rate monitoring recommended. Serotonin Syndrome. Increased Risk of Bleeding with NSAIDs/aspirin/anticoagulants. Severe Skin Reactions (erythema multiforme, SJS). Discontinuation Syndrome upon abrupt cessation. Activation of Mania/Hypomania. Angle-Closure Glaucoma. Seizures. Blood Pressure Increases. Urinary Hesitation and Retention.
sections.adverse_reactions: Most common adverse reactions (incidence >= 5% and at least twice placebo): nausea, dry mouth, somnolence, constipation, decreased appetite, hyperhidrosis, fatigue, and dizziness.
sections.drug_interactions: MAOIs: Contraindicated. Potent CYP1A2 Inhibitors (fluvoxamine, ciprofloxacin): Concomitant use should be avoided as it produces marked increases in duloxetine exposure. CYP2D6 Inhibitors (paroxetine, fluoxetine, quinidine): Increase duloxetine levels. Serotonergic Drugs: Risk of serotonin syndrome. Drugs affecting hemostasis (NSAIDs, warfarin): Increased bleeding risk.
sections.use_in_specific_populations: Pregnancy Category C: Neonates exposed to SNRIs late in the third trimester have developed complications requiring prolonged hospitalization. Lactation: Excreted in human breast milk. Hepatic Impairment: Avoid use in patients with chronic liver disease or cirrhosis. Severe Renal Impairment: Avoid use in end-stage renal disease (ESRD) or CrCl < 30 mL/min.
sections.overdosage: Fatalities have occurred in acute overdoses, independently and in combination with other drugs, with doses as low as 1000 mg. Symptoms include somnolence, coma, serotonin syndrome, seizures, syncope, tachycardia, hypotension, hypertension, and vomiting. Maintain airway and cardiac monitoring; no specific antidote.
sections.clinical_pharmacology: Duloxetine is a potent inhibitor of neuronal serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake and a weak inhibitor of dopamine reuptake. Duloxetine has no significant affinity for dopaminergic, adrenergic, cholinergic, histaminergic, opioid, glutamate, or GABA receptors in vitro. Extensively metabolized by CYP1A2 and CYP2D6.

sections.indications_and_usage: Omeprazole is a proton pump inhibitor indicated for: Treatment of active duodenal ulcer; Treatment of active benign gastric ulcer; Treatment of gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD); Maintenance of healing of erosive esophagitis; Pathological hypersecretory conditions (Zollinger-Ellison syndrome); Eradication of Helicobacter pylori in combination with clarithromycin and amoxicillin.
sections.dosage_and_administration: Take before eating, preferably in the morning. Swallow capsules whole; do not chew or crush. Active Duodenal Ulcer: 20 mg once daily for 4 weeks. Gastric Ulcer: 40 mg once daily for 4 to 8 weeks. GERD / Erosive Esophagitis: 20 mg once daily for 4 to 8 weeks. Zollinger-Ellison Syndrome: Starting dose is 60 mg once daily, adjusted up to 120 mg three times daily.
sections.contraindications: Known hypersensitivity to omeprazole or other substituted benzimidazoles (e.g., esomeprazole, lansoprazole, pantoprazole). Co-administration with rilpivirine-containing products.
sections.warnings_and_precautions: Gastric Malignancy: Symptomatic response to therapy does not preclude presence of gastric malignancy. Acute Tubulointerstitial Nephritis. Clostridioides difficile-Associated Diarrhea (CDAD). Bone Fracture: Long-term and multiple daily dose therapy associated with increased risk of osteoporosis-related fractures of hip, wrist, or spine. Cutaneous and Systemic Lupus Erythematosus. Vitamin B12 (Cyanocobalamin) Deficiency with daily long-term use (> 3 years). Hypomagnesemia with prolonged use (> 1 year). Fundic gland polyps.
sections.adverse_reactions: Most common adverse reactions (incidence >= 2%) in adults are headache, abdominal pain, nausea, diarrhea, vomiting, and flatulence. In pediatric patients: respiratory system events, fever.
sections.drug_interactions: Clopidogrel: Concomitant use reduces exposure to the active metabolite of clopidogrel and decreases antiplatelet activity; avoid co-administration. Drugs dependent on gastric pH for absorption (ketoconazole, iron salts, erlotinib, mycophenolate mofetil): Omeprazole decreases absorption. Diazepam, Warfarin, Phenytoin: Omeprazole inhibits CYP2C19 and may prolong elimination. Methotrexate: Concomitant PPI use may elevate and prolong methotrexate levels; consider temporary PPI withdrawal.
sections.use_in_specific_populations: Pregnancy Category C: Extensive epidemiological studies show no increased risk of major congenital malformations. Lactation: Excreted in human milk in low amounts. Hepatic Impairment: Increased bioavailability and half-life; consider dose reduction especially for maintenance of healing of erosive esophagitis.
sections.overdosage: Doses up to 2400 mg have been reported. Symptoms include confusion, drowsiness, blurred vision, tachycardia, nausea, vomiting, diaphoresis, flushing, headache, and dry mouth. Omeprazole is not readily dialyzable due to high protein binding (~ 95%). Treatment is supportive.
sections.clinical_pharmacology: Omeprazole is a substituted benzimidazole that suppresses gastric basal and stimulated acid secretion by specific inhibition of the H+/K+ ATPase enzyme system at the secretory surface of the gastric parietal cell. Extensively metabolized by CYP2C19 and CYP3A4.

sections.indications_and_usage: Protonix is a proton pump inhibitor indicated for: Short-term treatment (up to 8 weeks) in the healing and symptomatic relief of erosive esophagitis associated with gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD); Maintenance of healing of erosive esophagitis; Long-term treatment of pathological hypersecretory conditions, including Zollinger-Ellison syndrome.
sections.dosage_and_administration: Take with or without food. Swallow tablets whole; do not split, chew, or crush. Treatment of Erosive Esophagitis: 40 mg once daily for up to 8 weeks; an additional 8 weeks may be considered if unhealed. Maintenance of Healing: 40 mg once daily. Pathological Hypersecretion (Zollinger-Ellison): 40 mg twice daily, adjusted up to 240 mg daily.
sections.contraindications: Known hypersensitivity to pantoprazole or substituted benzimidazoles. Co-administration with rilpivirine-containing products.
sections.warnings_and_precautions: Presence of gastric malignancy not ruled out by symptomatic response. Acute tubulointerstitial nephritis. Clostridioides difficile-associated diarrhea (CDAD). Increased risk of osteoporosis-related fractures of hip, wrist, or spine with high-dose long-term use. Severe cutaneous adverse reactions (SCAR / SJS / TEN). Cutaneous and systemic lupus erythematosus. Cyanocobalamin (Vitamin B12) deficiency with long-term therapy. Hypomagnesemia with long-term therapy.
sections.adverse_reactions: Most common adverse reactions (incidence >= 2%) include headache, diarrhea, nausea, abdominal pain, vomiting, flatulence, dizziness, and arthralgia.
sections.drug_interactions: Rilpivirine, atazanavir, nelfinavir: Concomitant use contraindicated due to loss of antiviral efficacy. Warfarin: Monitor INR/prothrombin time; increases in INR reported. Methotrexate: Elevated serum levels. Drugs dependent on gastric pH (ketoconazole, iron salts): Decreased absorption. Clopidogrel: Pantoprazole has less inhibitory effect on CYP2C19 than omeprazole.
sections.use_in_specific_populations: Pregnancy Category B: Studies in animals show no evidence of harm to the fetus. Lactation: Excreted in human milk; use only if benefit outweighs risk. Pediatric Use: Approved for healing erosive esophagitis in patients 5 years and older.
sections.overdosage: Doses up to 240 mg intravenously have been administered without adverse effects. Pantoprazole is not removed by hemodialysis. Treatment should be symptomatic and supportive.
sections.clinical_pharmacology: Pantoprazole is a substituted benzimidazole that suppresses gastric acid secretion by irreversibly inhibiting the gastric H+/K+-ATPase pump in gastric parietal cells. Extensively metabolized by the liver, primarily by CYP2C19 with minor contributions from CYP3A4, CYP2D6, and CYP2C9.

sections.indications_and_usage: Ondansetron is a 5-HT3 receptor antagonist indicated for: Prevention of nausea and vomiting associated with highly emetogenic cancer chemotherapy (HEC); Prevention of nausea and vomiting associated with moderately emetogenic cancer chemotherapy (MEC); Prevention of nausea and vomiting associated with radiation therapy (total body irradiation, single high-dose fraction, or daily fractions); Prevention of postoperative nausea and vomiting (PONV).
sections.dosage_and_administration: Highly Emetogenic Chemotherapy (HEC): Single 24 mg dose taken 30 minutes before start of single-day chemotherapy. Moderately Emetogenic Chemotherapy (MEC): 8 mg dose taken 30 minutes before chemotherapy, followed by 8 mg 8 hours after initial dose, then 8 mg twice daily for 1 to 2 days. Radiation Therapy: 8 mg 1 to 2 hours before radiation. PONV: 16 mg orally 1 hour before induction of anesthesia. In severe hepatic impairment (Child-Pugh score >= 10), total daily dose should not exceed 8 mg.
sections.contraindications: Concomitant use of apomorphine (causes profound hypotension and loss of consciousness). Known hypersensitivity to ondansetron.
sections.warnings_and_precautions: QT Interval Prolongation and Torsades de Pointes: Dose-dependent QT prolongation; avoid in patients with congenital long QT syndrome. Serotonin Syndrome: Reported when used in combination with other serotonergic drugs (SSRIs, SNRIs, MAOIs, triptans). Myocardial Ischemia: Coronary artery vasospasm reported. Masking of Progressive Ileus and Gastric Distention after abdominal surgery.
sections.adverse_reactions: Most common adverse reactions (incidence >= 5%) in adults include headache, constipation, fatigue, malaise, diarrhea, dizziness, and drowsiness.
sections.drug_interactions: Apomorphine: Contraindicated due to risk of profound hypotension. Serotonergic Drugs (SSRIs, SNRIs, TCAs, MAOIs): Increased risk of serotonin syndrome. CYP3A4 Inducers (rifampin, phenytoin, carbamazepine): Increase ondansetron clearance and decrease blood concentrations. Antiarrhythmics (amiodarone) and other QT-prolonging drugs: Additive risk of QT prolongation.
sections.use_in_specific_populations: Pregnancy Category B: Published epidemiological studies do not establish a drug-associated risk of adverse maternal or fetal outcomes. Lactation: Present in rat milk; not known if excreted in human milk. Hepatic Impairment: Do not exceed 8 mg/day in severe hepatic impairment.
sections.overdosage: Doses over 10 times the recommended dose have been ingested. Symptoms include sudden blindness (amaurosis) of 2-3 minutes duration, severe constipation, hypotension, vasovagal episode with transient second-degree heart block, and serotonin syndrome. There is no specific antidote; hemodialysis is not effective.
sections.clinical_pharmacology: Ondansetron is a selective 5-HT3 receptor antagonist. Chemotherapeutic agents and radiotherapy cause release of serotonin (5-HT) from enterochromaffin cells of the small intestine, initiating the vomiting reflex via vagal afferents. Ondansetron blocks 5-HT3 receptors both peripherally on vagal nerve terminals and centrally in the chemoreceptor trigger zone (CTZ). Extensively metabolized by CYP3A4, CYP1A2, and CYP2D6.

sections.boxed_warning: WARNING: ADDICTION, ABUSE, AND MISUSE; RISK EVALUATION AND MITIGATION STRATEGY (REMS); LIFE-THREATENING RESPIRATORY DEPRESSION; ACCIDENTAL INGESTION; ULTRA-RAPID METABOLISM OF TRAMADOL AND OTHER RISK FACTORS FOR LIFE-THREATENING RESPIRATORY DEPRESSION IN CHILDREN; NEONATAL OPIOID WITHDRAWAL SYNDROME; INTERACTIONS WITH DRUGS AFFECTING CYTOCHROME P450 ISOENZYMES; AND RISKS FROM CONCOMITANT USE WITH BENZODIAZEPINES OR OTHER CNS DEPRESSANTS. Tramadol exposes patients and other users to the risks of opioid addiction, abuse, and misuse. Serious, life-threatening, or fatal respiratory depression may occur. Concomitant use with benzodiazepines or other CNS depressants may result in profound sedation, respiratory depression, coma, and death. Life-threatening respiratory depression and death have occurred in children who received tramadol who were ultra-rapid metabolizers of tramadol due to a CYP2D6 polymorphism.
sections.indications_and_usage: Tramadol hydrochloride tablets are indicated in adults for the management of pain severe enough to require an opioid analgesic and for which alternative treatments are inadequate.
sections.dosage_and_administration: Immediate-Release: 50 mg to 100 mg orally every 4 to 6 hours as needed for pain relief. Maximum daily dose is 400 mg per day. In patients over 75 years of age, maximum recommended dose is 300 mg/day in divided doses. Renal Impairment (CrCl < 30 mL/min): Increase dosing interval to every 12 hours (maximum 200 mg/day). Severe Hepatic Impairment (cirrhosis): 50 mg every 12 hours.
sections.contraindications: Children younger than 12 years of age. Postoperative management in children younger than 18 years following tonsillectomy or adenoidectomy. Significant respiratory depression. Acute or severe bronchial asthma. Known or suspected gastrointestinal obstruction, including paralytic ileus. Concomitant use of monoamine oxidase inhibitors (MAOIs) or use within the last 14 days.
sections.warnings_and_precautions: Addiction, abuse, and misuse. Life-threatening respiratory depression. Ultra-rapid CYP2D6 metabolism leading to opioid toxicity in children and nursing infants. Neonatal opioid withdrawal syndrome. Severe hypotension. Serotonin Syndrome: Potentially life-threatening when co-administered with serotonergic drugs (SSRIs, SNRIs, triptans, TCAs). Seizure Risk: Can cause seizures; risk increased in patients taking medications that lower seizure threshold (antidepressants, neuroleptics) or with history of seizures. Suicide Risk. Adrenal Insufficiency.
sections.adverse_reactions: Most common adverse reactions (incidence >= 5%) are dizziness, vertigo, nausea, constipation, headache, somnolence, vomiting, pruritus, CNS stimulation, asthenia, sweating, dyspepsia, and dry mouth.
sections.drug_interactions: Serotonergic Drugs (SSRIs, SNRIs, MAOIs, triptans): High risk of serotonin syndrome. Benzodiazepines and CNS Depressants: Profound sedation and respiratory depression. CYP2D6 Inhibitors (quinidine, fluoxetine, paroxetine, bupropion): Increase tramadol concentrations and reduce active M1 metabolite. CYP3A4 Inhibitors (erythromycin, ketoconazole) / Inducers (rifampin, carbamazepine).
sections.use_in_specific_populations: Pregnancy: Prolonged use during pregnancy can cause neonatal opioid withdrawal syndrome. Lactation: Breastfeeding is not recommended due to risk of serious adverse reactions, including excess sleepiness, difficulty breastfeeding, or fatal respiratory depression in infant. Pediatric Use: Contraindicated in children < 12 years.
sections.overdosage: Acute overdosage manifests by respiratory depression, somnolence progressing to stupor or coma, flaccid skeletal muscles, cold and clammy skin, constricted pupils, bradycardia, hypotension, and death. Naloxone administration is indicated for respiratory depression, but naloxone increases the risk of seizures in tramadol overdose.
sections.clinical_pharmacology: Tramadol is a centrally acting synthetic opioid analgesic. Its mode of action involves two complementary mechanisms: weak binding to mu-opioid receptors and inhibition of reuptake of norepinephrine and serotonin. Metabolized in the liver by CYP2D6 to the active metabolite O-desmethyltramadol (M1), which has a higher affinity for mu-opioid receptors than the parent drug.
